DEEP MOTEL

"The Ledger" · a neon-noir lyric film · 16:9 cinematic · John Wick palette

This started as concept art for a friend who reached out about possibly making a video for his song, for these lyrics. This is what we imagined for him.

We are sharing it here because it is also a working example of your method, Andries: the Visual Director six layers, applied end to end.

the cast + the world · 16:9 cinematic · this is how it is built

What the video is about

The song is a motel guest ledger: every verse a room, every room a small anonymous story where nobody uses a real name. The film makes that literal · one neon motel across one long night, one figure (the night clerk) keeping the record. The rule is a John Wick inversion of comfort: darkness is safe, sunrise is the threat, and the light warms from cyan toward gold as the danger closes in.

The look · mood & palette

John Wick as the north star: rain-slick blacks, teal-and-magenta neon, one hot accent per frame. These are the reference boards we're grading toward.

The direction we chose · The Ledger

We sketched a few possible directions and chose this one. It stays the tightest to the song and the cheapest to stage.

DIRECTION 01

The Ledger

Clerk's POV. One motel, one night, room by room · each number a 3-second vignette of a different anonymous couple. The numbered lyric structure is the edit. One consistent face (the clerk) threading total anonymity. Cheapest to stage, tightest to the song.

Your method, the six layers

We built this whole thing the way you teach it, Andries. Every image is stacked from six named layers, and the core move is always the same: translate every feeling into named physics. Here are the six layers, the way we used them.

Andries' six-layer method

The Visual Director
1 · SubjectWho or what the frame is about, named specifically instead of vaguely.
2 · CameraLens, aperture, angle. The eye, and exactly how it sees.
3 · LightingSource, direction, quality, Kelvin. Mood written as physics.
4 · MaterialsSurface, finish, texture. What each thing is actually made of.
5 · CompositionPlacement and negative space. Where everything sits in the frame.
6 · StyleReference and grade. The finished look we are pointing at.
Core ruleTranslate every feeling into named physics.

Woman in Red · the Serpent Necklace woman

She did not start as a music-video character. We built her from scratch first, as a fine-art editorial luxury-jewelry shot, using your six layers to take her from "just a woman in a red dress" all the way up to full detail. That finished image became her face-lock reference, and from it we generated the five-angle character sheet shown here for this campaign.

Woman in RedThe Never-Heres · Her
The real prompt that made her (v2, trimmed). "Fine-art editorial luxury jewelry campaign photograph, studio-controlled, cinematic chiaroscuro against a deep near-black background. A very tan woman with long wavy dark-blonde honey-balayage hair. She sits on the studio floor, knees folded, wearing an intensely red silk suit set with a deep plunging neckline. She wears the gold serpent necklace against her bare chest. Medium-wide, 50mm, f/2.8, eye-level. She occupies about 45 percent of the frame, lower-right third, generous dark negative space to the upper-left. Single hard directional key from screen-left ~5000K, deep falloff into black. The necklace is ancient, opaque, matte antique gold, richly textured segmented snake-scale surface, low specular, two serpents crossing, ruby cabochon eyes glowing with deep internal gemstone light like sun through a real ruby. Red silk shows a liquid sheen with soft speculars over the folds. Skin hyperreal, sun-kissed tan, warm subsurface glow, visible pores. Color story: crimson red, antique gold, warm tan, near-black. Subtle film grain, painterly negative space."

We used this same woman, with her necklace details, in the campaign, and built her five-angle character sheet from everything the method taught us.

Character sheets · how the cast is built

Every character is one composite sheet: five angles (face · front · back · left · right) plus a data card, on a neutral background so the identity reads clean. The method is reference-locked: we feed a face reference and one locked template sheet into Nano Banana Pro (Magnific), so every sheet in the cast comes out identical. Neon is saved for the scene stills. Below is the Stray, with the exact prompt that made him.

The StrayThe Never-Heres · Him
Built from: a locked template sheet (format), text identity → Nano Banana Pro → 16:9. (v2, repaired for a healthier read.) Prompt: Reference sheet, 5 labeled panels matching the template. Camera: full-frame, 85mm, f/5.6, ISO 200. Subject: ruggedly handsome man mid-40s, fit and healthy, athletic lean-muscular, upright posture, light tan, tousled dark hair with grey at the temples, groomed short stubble, alert magnetic eyes, lightly worn from one great late night, a charismatic frontman who takes care of himself. Wardrobe neat-but-undone: charcoal open shirt over a fitted white tee, slim dark jeans, worn boots, thin silver chain. Negatives: NOT gaunt, sickly, junkie or slouched. No neon, no logos, no watermark. Identical across panels.

Next in the pipeline: another sheet or two, then a few neon scene stills, then video. Nothing generates without a go.

The Rooms · diagnosing and repairing a frame

The method is not only for building an image from nothing. It is also how we fix one. In one room scene we rendered, the nightstand held two whisky glasses and a bottle, which did not make sense for the story: only one person was drinking. We did not re-roll the whole frame and hope the model would sort it out. We edited it part by part, little by little, layer by layer, taking out only the second glass while locking everything else in place: both characters, the camera, the light, the materials. Change the one thing that is wrong, keep the rest named and still.

Before · what was off

the diagnosis
SubjectBoth characters in the room, but two glasses on the table where the story wants only one.
CompositionThe extra glass pulled the eye and implied a second drinker who is not in the scene.
The planKeep every other layer locked (camera, light, materials, both characters) and touch only the one wrong element.

After · the repair

the render
EditWe named the exact change in the same six-layer language and re-rendered: both characters, one glass on the table, nothing else moved.
Why it holdsBecause every other layer stayed named and fixed, the model had nothing to drift on. The physics held; only the glass changed.
TakeawayA frame is never simply "wrong," a layer was under-specified. Name the layer, fix the frame.

Both frames above are the real renders, before and after the one-glass fix.
